narrative:
The model predicted a 77% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year ranking also pulled the outcome in the same direction, though with less force. These two performance measures outweighed everything else.

Your undergraduate GPA was the only notable factor that worked in your favor, pulling the prediction slightly toward passing. However, its positive effect was not nearly large enough to offset the impact of your low class rankings.

Compared with students who were accepted, your first- and third-year decile rankings of 1 were far below the typical averages of around 6 and 5.8, and your undergraduate GPA of 2.10 sat well under the accepted students’ average of 3.23. Your LSAT score of 30 was also noticeably below the accepted average of 37.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT. Stronger grades and a higher test score in a future application would directly address the factors that led to this rejection.
